LONDON, England -- A severe rabies epidemic has claimed the lives of at least 83 children within three months in Angola's capital, Luanda, the World Health Organization (WHO) has said. Luanda, which has a large population of stray dogs, also has some of the world's worst slums. Some of the children were also brought into the hospital too late to be saved, Luis Bernardino, head of the hospital told UN humanitarian organization IRIN. He warned that the number of deaths could be much higher. "The children were brought to our hospital and are the only ones we know of, so the number could be higher," Bernardino told IRIN. "It is a sad moment for us," he added. "I think it was probably that no one was prepared for such a high case load." The number of cases has now started declining, however, said Bernardino. According to Meslin, this could be because the current infected pack of dogs has died. Meslin told CNN that the Angolan government needed to embark on a dog rabies control program urgently to prevent further outbreaks. Angola's capital, where most of the population live in slums, has a large number of stray dogs who are said to have caused the epidemic. "We have had some sporadic cases in other provincial capitals in the country; we think the virus was brought into Luanda and then spread through the dogs -- Angolans love dogs," Bernardino said. "When the first 10 deaths were reported in December 2008 we alerted the authorities, but we do not have veterinary services in the city, no kennels [to keep and observe the animals] and vaccinate them," he added. Another problem contributing to the crisis is that vaccines are too expensive for the average family. "One dose of vaccine costs about $10 and five of those have to be administered, which makes the total cost of treatment $50 which is more than a month's salary for families in most developing countries," Meslin added. In 2008 the WHO wrote that rabies, a disease transmitted from animals with infected saliva to humans, is present on nearly every continent of the world but more that 95 per cent of human deaths occur in Asia and Africa. It can be prevented by vaccination, either prior to exposure or as part of post-exposure treatment. But once symptoms of the disease develop, rabies is fatal. According to the WHO, rabies can affect the lungs, stomach and central nervous systems. In the critical stage, a victim slips into a coma and death, usually due to breathing failure. More than 55,000 people die of rabies each year, the WHO wrote, with 30 to 60 per cent of the victims of dog bites being children under the age of 15.

A devastating rabies epidemic has swept through Luanda, the capital of Angola, killing at least 83 children over the course of just three months, according to figures released by the World Health Organization. The scale of this outbreak has raised serious alarm among global health officials, who fear the true human toll may be far greater than currently documented.

Francois Meslin, a rabies expert with the WHO, has cautioned that the reported death toll likely represents only a fraction of the actual devastation caused by the outbreak. "This could be just the tip of the iceberg," Meslin warned, suggesting that many more cases may have gone unreported or unrecorded, particularly in areas with limited access to healthcare infrastructure or diagnostic capabilities.

The crisis was compounded by a critical failure in the local healthcare response. At Luanda's largest referral hospital, medical staff found themselves powerless to save any of the children brought in with rabies symptoms. The hospital had completely exhausted its supply of rabies vaccines, leaving healthcare workers without the essential tools needed to treat the disease. Adding to this tragedy, some children arrived at the hospital only after the infection had progressed too far, by which point treatment would have been futile regardless of vaccine availability. Once symptoms of rabies appear, the disease is almost universally fatal, underscoring the critical importance of timely post-exposure treatment.

At the root of this public health disaster lies Luanda's substantial population of stray and free-roaming dogs, which serve as the primary vector for rabies transmission to humans. This problem has been significantly exacerbated by systemic gaps in the city's infrastructure for managing animal-borne diseases. Luanda lacks adequate veterinary services to monitor and treat animal populations, has no proper kennel facilities where potentially rabid animals could be observed and quarantined, and suffers from a scarcity of affordable vaccines—both for the animal population and for human post-exposure prophylaxis. These combined deficiencies created ideal conditions for the rapid spread of the disease throughout the city.

There is a glimmer of hope amid this crisis, as health officials have observed a recent decline in the number of new rabies cases. Some experts speculate that this downturn may be attributable to the natural die-off of the specific pack of infected dogs responsible for the initial wave of transmissions. However, public health specialists caution against interpreting this decline as a sign that the underlying problem has been resolved.

Experts are now urging the Angolan government to take decisive and immediate action by implementing a comprehensive dog rabies control program. Such a program would need to address the root causes of the epidemic, including establishing reliable veterinary services, creating proper animal observation and quarantine facilities, and ensuring consistent access to affordable vaccines for both animals and at-risk human populations. Without these systemic interventions, health officials warn that Luanda remains vulnerable to future outbreaks that could once again put the city's most vulnerable population—its children—at grave risk.

**LUANDA, Angola** — A deadly rabies outbreak has swept through Angola's capital, killing dozens of children in recent weeks and exposing critical gaps in the country's public health infrastructure, according to local health officials and the World Health Organization.

Health authorities in Luanda Province report that the majority of victims are children under the age of 15, many of whom were bitten by stray or unvaccinated dogs in densely populated neighborhoods on the city's outskirts. Officials say delays in seeking treatment, combined with limited availability of post-exposure vaccines, have contributed to the mounting death toll.

"Rabies is almost universally fatal once symptoms appear, but it is also almost entirely preventable," said a WHO representative for the Africa region in a statement released this week. "The tragedy unfolding in Luanda underscores what happens when community awareness, animal vaccination programs, and access to post-exposure prophylaxis all fall short at the same time."

## A Preventable Crisis

Rabies is transmitted primarily through the bites or scratches of infected animals, with dogs responsible for up to 99% of human cases worldwide, according to the WHO. The disease is fatal in nearly all cases once clinical symptoms — including fever, confusion, and hydrophobia — begin to appear. However, timely administration of post-exposure vaccines can prevent the disease entirely, even after a bite.

Angolan health officials say the outbreak has been exacerbated by a combination of factors: a large population of unvaccinated stray dogs, limited public awareness about the urgency of seeking treatment after animal bites, and shortages of rabies vaccines and immunoglobulin at local clinics.

"Many parents did not realize that a simple dog bite could be fatal," said a spokesperson for Angola's Ministry of Health. "By the time some children showed symptoms, it was already too late."

## WHO Sounds the Alarm

The WHO has pledged to support Angola's government with emergency vaccine shipments, technical guidance, and public education campaigns. The organization emphasized that mass dog vaccination campaigns are the most effective long-term solution to preventing future outbreaks.

"We are working closely with Angolan authorities to scale up access to life-saving post-exposure vaccines and to launch mass dog vaccination drives in affected communities," the WHO statement continued. "Our goal, alongside global partners, remains eliminating dog-mediated human rabies deaths by 2030."

The WHO, along with partner organizations including the Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Organisation for Animal Health, has long promoted a "One Health" approach to rabies elimination — one that combines animal vaccination, human treatment access, and community education.

## Community Impact

Residents in affected neighborhoods described a growing sense of fear and grief. Community leaders have called on the government to expedite emergency vaccine distribution and to launch awareness campaigns in schools and local markets.

"We are burying children who should be alive," one community leader in Luanda told reporters. "This didn't have to happen."

Local clinics have reportedly been overwhelmed, with some families traveling long distances in search of available treatment. Health workers have urged anyone bitten or scratched by an animal — even one that appears healthy — to seek medical attention immediately.

## Moving Forward

Angolan officials say emergency response teams have been deployed to the hardest-hit districts, and mobile vaccination units for both humans and animals are being rolled out in the coming days. The WHO has urged the international community to assist with funding and vaccine supplies as the country works to contain the outbreak.

Public health experts warn that without sustained investment in dog vaccination programs and public education, similar outbreaks could recur in other under-resourced urban areas across the region.

"This is a solvable problem," the WHO statement concluded. "No child should die from a disease we know how to prevent."

**LUANDA, Angola** — Health authorities in Angola's capital are grappling with a severe rabies outbreak that has affected 83 children in recent months, prompting urgent warnings from public health officials and renewed scrutiny of the country's animal vaccination infrastructure.

## A Growing Crisis

Provincial health department officials confirmed that the cases have emerged primarily from densely populated neighborhoods on Luanda's outskirts, where stray dog populations have surged in recent years. Children, who are statistically more likely to approach unfamiliar animals and less likely to report bites immediately, have borne the brunt of the exposure.

"Rabies is almost universally fatal once symptoms appear, which is why post-exposure treatment within hours of a bite is critical," said a spokesperson for Angola's National Directorate of Public Health. "The tragedy here is that this disease is entirely preventable."

## Root Causes: A Perfect Storm

Health officials and veterinary experts point to several converging factors behind the outbreak:

**Uncontrolled Stray Dog Populations**
Luanda's rapid urbanization has outpaced municipal capacity to manage animal populations. Informal settlements on the city's periphery have seen dog populations multiply largely unchecked, with limited spaying, neutering, or vaccination coverage.

**Vaccine Shortages**
Perhaps most alarming to health workers is a persistent shortage of both human post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) treatment and canine rabies vaccines. Clinics in several districts have reported running out of immunoglobulin and vaccine doses for weeks at a time, forcing families to travel long distances or go without timely treatment. Supply chain disruptions and budget constraints have been cited as contributing factors.

**Limited Public Awareness**
Community health workers note that many families remain unaware of the urgency of seeking treatment immediately after a bite, sometimes waiting days before seeking care—a delay that can prove fatal once the virus reaches the nervous system.

## WHO Sounds the Alarm

The World Health Organization has issued statements urging Angolan authorities to scale up emergency response measures, calling the situation "a preventable public health failure." The WHO has emphasized that:

- Mass dog vaccination campaigns covering at least 70% of the dog population are essential to break transmission cycles
- Reliable stockpiles of human vaccines must be maintained in high-risk urban areas
- Rabies remains one of the most neglected tropical diseases despite being 100% preventable with timely intervention

The organization has offered technical support and has called on international donors to assist with emergency vaccine procurement.

## Government Response

In response to mounting pressure, Angola's Ministry of Health has announced plans for an emergency vaccination drive targeting both stray and owned dogs across Luanda province, alongside efforts to replenish human vaccine stocks. Officials have also pledged public awareness campaigns in affected communities, particularly targeting schools.

However, critics argue the response has been slow, with some community leaders demanding more immediate and sustained investment in veterinary public health infrastructure.

As the death toll and case count continue to be assessed, public health experts stress that Luanda's outbreak reflects a broader challenge facing many rapidly growing African cities: balancing urban development with adequate public health safeguards.

**LUANDA, Angola** — Angola's capital city faced a significant public health challenge in 2009 as rabies cases surged, prompting health officials to sound the alarm and launch emergency response measures to contain the deadly viral disease.

- **Bites from infected animals** — most commonly dogs in urban African settings

2. **Public education** about avoiding contact with stray animals and seeking immediate treatment after bites

- Limited availability of rabies vaccines in some clinics
- Public awareness gaps about the importance of seeking treatment immediately after animal bites

- The logistical difficulty of managing large populations of stray dogs in a rapidly urbanizing capital

**LUANDA, Angola** — A surge in rabies cases has put Angola's capital on high alert, as health authorities confront a rising death toll, overwhelmed medical facilities, and a public struggling to afford life-saving vaccines.

## Death Toll Mounts

Health officials in Luanda have reported a troubling increase in rabies fatalities in recent months, with victims including a disproportionate number of children who are more likely to be bitten by infected animals and less likely to report exposure promptly. Local hospitals have confirmed multiple deaths from the viral disease, which is almost universally fatal once clinical symptoms appear. Health workers say the true number of cases may be underreported, as many residents in outlying communities lack easy access to diagnostic and treatment centers.

## Hospitals Under Pressure

Major health facilities in Luanda, including the Hospital Américo Boavida, have reported being stretched thin by the influx of patients seeking post-exposure treatment following dog bites. Medical staff describe shortages of anti-rabies immunoglobulin and inconsistent vaccine supplies, forcing some patients to travel between facilities in search of treatment. Emergency rooms have seen a spike in patients presenting with animal bites, many of whom delayed seeking care due to cost concerns or lack of awareness about rabies risks.

Doctors have called on the government to bolster stockpiles and streamline distribution to prevent treatment gaps, warning that any delay in administering post-exposure prophylaxis can prove fatal once symptoms begin.

## The Cost Barrier

A central obstacle to controlling the outbreak has been the price of rabies vaccines, which remain out of reach for many Angolan families. A full course of post-exposure prophylaxis — typically requiring multiple doses over several weeks, sometimes alongside costly immunoglobulin — can run into tens of thousands of kwanzas, a substantial burden in a country where a significant share of the population lives on a limited income. Public health advocates argue that without subsidies or free distribution through public hospitals, poorer residents will continue to forgo timely treatment, raising the risk of preventable deaths.

Veterinary vaccination campaigns for dogs, considered the most cost-effective way to interrupt transmission at its source, have also faced funding and logistical challenges, including limited outreach in informal settlements where stray and unvaccinated dogs are common.

## A Global Health Burden

The outbreak in Luanda echoes a persistent global challenge. According to the World Health Organization, rabies is present in more than 150 countries and territories, and claims an estimated 59,000 lives every year — a toll that falls disproportionately on Africa and Asia. The WHO notes that dogs are responsible for up to 99% of human rabies transmissions, and that children under 15 account for nearly 40% of victims worldwide, largely due to their higher likelihood of contact with animals and lower likelihood of reporting bites.

The organization emphasizes that rabies is virtually 100% preventable through timely vaccination, yet access barriers — cost, availability, and awareness — continue to drive fatalities in lower-income regions. WHO has set a global target, alongside partner organizations, to eliminate dog-mediated human rabies deaths by 2030 through mass canine vaccination, improved access to human vaccines, and public education campaigns.

## Looking Ahead

Public health experts in Angola are urging a coordinated response that combines expanded vaccine access, mass dog vaccination drives, and community education about bite prevention and prompt treatment-seeking. Without such measures, they warn, Luanda's outbreak could continue to claim lives that modern medicine has long been able to prevent.
